_meta.description: Mintago cadence playbook. Encodes the FORM of the 4-email outbound sequence (subject/body/formatting mechanics, altitude-tier tone, persona tone-by-seniority, per-step structure) as distinct from config/signal-substance.json, which encodes the ANGLE/content of a given signal. Both are loaded into the same generation prompt as clearly separate labeled sections.
_meta.notes_on_word_counts: Steps 2-4 were specified by the architect as sentence counts (2-4 / 3-4 / 2-3 sentences) rather than word counts. Each step below carries an authoritative sentence_count_range, plus a word_count_range that is a documented approximation (~12 words/sentence average) used only for the advisory, non-blocking word-count flag computed on read. Step 1 was specified directly as a 25-50 word range and uses that as its authoritative word_count_range.
_meta._deprecated: Superseded by config/claygent-prompt.md as of the Claygent prompt integration. No longer used in the active generation path. Kept for reference.

universal_subject_rules.tone: neutral, factual — reads like an internal to-do item
rules: Only include the company name if there is an existing relationship
Personalize against a real, verifiable signal
25-80 words target, with 25-50 being the peak/sweet spot
Write to start a conversation, not to inform
CTA must be low-friction, closed-ended, and specific enough to answer yes/no
Follow-up emails restate the original reason for reaching out before adding anything new
Never more than one open-ended question per email
avoid: Long intros or walls of text
Multiple value props stacked in one email
Presumptive framing (turn it into a question instead)

rules: Greeting is first name + comma only (no 'Hi'/'Hello')
Sign-off is first name only ("Tom") — no title, company, or signature block
P.S. lines (when used) are tied to the referral ask or a callback to the original reason, one line only
Don't use bullets unless the content genuinely benefits from them

Executive.guidance: Anchor on a company-level strategic trigger. Frame the outcome as cost, risk, or time at the org level. Offer a delegation path — an explicit way to hand this to whoever owns it day-to-day.

Director.titles_example: Director / Senior manager who owns a function
Director.guidance: Anchor on the specific function or program they own, not company-wide strategy.

Manager.guidance: Anchor on the weekly process they run. Practical and tactical, not strategic.

IC.guidance: Anchor on the specific task eating their day. Shortest, most casual tone of any tier.

HR.overview: Warm, human-centered tone. Lead with specific pain points. Use a brevity + benefit framing. Keep the CTA simple.

Executive.titles_example: CHRO / VP People / Head of People
Executive.guidance: Company-level observation -> people challenge at their stage -> people-first outcome framing (retention/culture/manager quality). Short and human. Offer to delegate down.

Director.titles_example: Director of People Ops / Talent / Employee Experience
Director.guidance: Anchor on a specific program (onboarding, performance cycles, engagement surveys, talent reviews). Use proof from a similar-stage company. Do not use 'transform your HR function' framing.

Manager.titles_example: HR Manager / People Ops Manager / Benefits Manager
Manager.guidance: Anchor on one workflow they run. Friendly-professional tone. Give a concrete next step, not 'thoughts?'. Short, scannable paragraphs.

IC.guidance: Warmest tone of the persona. Name the exact task/workflow. Tangible immediate benefit (e.g. 'saves 3 hrs/week'). Low-stakes CTA. Never imply buying authority.

Finance.overview: Numbers, precision, and clarity. Punishes vague, hyped, or abstract language. Use outcome/numbers framing, risk-reduction/compliance relevance, direct and concise copy, and low-friction closed asks.

Executive.titles_example: CFO / VP Finance / Head of Finance / Controller
Executive.guidance: Financial trigger (fundraise, headcount growth, office expansion, compliance deadline) -> cost/efficiency problem at that stage -> ONE contextualized proof point. Measured tone — zero hype, zero exclamation points. Offer to delegate to the day-to-day owner.

Director.titles_example: Director of FP&A / Finance / Accounting / Treasury
Director.guidance: Anchor on a specific function (forecasting accuracy, budget variance, close process, reconciliation). Anchor on the visible signal. One example with real numbers.

Manager.titles_example: Finance Manager / AP-AR Manager / Payroll Manager
Manager.guidance: Anchor on one process they own. Quantify the friction and the outcome. Tone: a peer who found a better way. Mobile-scannable.

IC.titles_example: Financial Analyst / Staff Accountant / AP-AR Specialist
IC.guidance: Shortest, plainest tone of the persona. Name the exact task eating their afternoon. No jargon, no ROI/strategy language. Goal is a conversation or an intro upward, not a close.

Ops.overview: Responds to a NAMED, SPECIFIC process, not a category or 'workflow challenge' — vague pain-point guesses backfire more with this persona than any other. Use efficiency framing tied to a concrete workflow, short direct emails, credibility signals, and a straightforward CTA.
avoid: Abstract strategy without a process anchor
Presumptive language — turn it into a question instead (e.g. 'How are you handling X as you scale?')

Executive.titles_example: COO / VP Ops / Head of Ops
Executive.guidance: Company-level scaling signal (headcount growth, new products, new offices, new segments) -> operational bottleneck at that stage. Direct/efficient tone, no rapport-building preamble. Under 100 words. Offer to delegate. Ask, don't assume.

Director.titles_example: Director of Ops / RevOps / Customer Ops
Director.guidance: Name a specific operational domain (onboarding workflows, data hygiene, cross-functional handoffs). One proof point. Frame the CTA as 'compare approaches'.

Manager.titles_example: Operations Manager / Process Manager / Implementation Manager
Manager.guidance: Anchor on one process they run. Be direct about what you solve. Quantify the outcome. Specific CTA tied to the exact workflow.

IC.guidance: Most casual tone of the persona. Name the exact task. No 'operational excellence' jargon. CTA can be implicit.

CEO.overview: Company-level trigger, not departmental detail. Frame the outcome as growth, cost, risk, or time. Brevity is non-negotiable. No product features or technical detail. Always offer an explicit delegation path. Zero hype, zero exclamation points. For SME/owner-operator CEOs, a slightly more specific/tactical hook can land, while keeping the brevity and non-hyped tone.
CEO.structure: 1-line trigger/observation -> 1-line company-level implication -> 1 proof point -> CTA with a delegation option.

Executive.guidance: Company-level trigger -> company-level implication (growth/cost/risk/time) -> one proof point -> CTA offering a delegation path. Brevity non-negotiable. No product features or technical detail. Zero hype.

Director.guidance: Rare for this persona, but if present, treat similarly to Executive with a slightly more tactical hook, keeping brevity and non-hyped tone.

Manager.guidance: Rare for this persona, but if present, treat similarly to Executive with a slightly more tactical hook, keeping brevity and non-hyped tone.

IC.guidance: Rare for this persona, but if present, treat similarly to Executive with a slightly more tactical hook, keeping brevity and non-hyped tone.

MD.overview: Managing Director. At true SME scale, an MD is often the same profile as a founder-CEO — apply the CEO guidance almost directly. Where the company has both an MD and separate ownership/a board, the MD is closer to an execution-focused 'Head of' role — lean slightly more tactical/specific than pure CEO guidance while keeping executive brevity. Because MDs at smaller companies often personally own HR/finance/ops decisions simultaneously, the strongest angle is usually the CROSS-FUNCTIONAL COST of a fragmented setup rather than a single-department pitch.
MD.structure: Company-stage trigger -> cross-functional cost/risk implication -> one concrete comparable-company proof point -> CTA offering a direct conversation or a path to whoever handles the day-to-day.

Executive.guidance: Company-stage trigger -> cross-functional cost/risk implication (not single-department) -> one concrete comparable-company proof point -> CTA offering either a direct conversation or a path to whoever handles day-to-day. If this MD is effectively a founder-CEO at true SME scale, lean on the CEO structure directly; if there is separate ownership/a board, lean slightly more tactical/specific while keeping executive brevity.

Director.guidance: Treat as Executive-tier guidance above; MD does not typically appear below Executive altitude.

Manager.guidance: Treat as Executive-tier guidance above; MD does not typically appear below Executive altitude.

IC.guidance: Treat as Executive-tier guidance above; MD does not typically appear below Executive altitude.

steps.label: cold_open
steps.framework: Observation -> Problem/Insight -> Proof point -> Solution -> CTA
special_rules: Open with the signal as a specific observation, not an assumption stated as fact — frame as 'curious if...' or 'am I off thinking...'
One sentence tying the observation to the likely problem
Exactly ONE proof point (a number, or a comparable company/stage) — no more
One plain-language solution sentence — no feature list
The goal is a reply, not a meeting — do not pitch a demo

steps.label: resource_share
special_rules: Reference a genuinely relevant third-party resource — NOT Mintago's own content
If no specific real resource is known/available, explicitly note that in the prompt rather than inventing a fake source or title
Briefly explain why the resource is relevant, tying back to the original signal
Soft close nodding back to email 1, e.g. 'Any thoughts on my last note?'

steps.label: clarification
steps.framework: Restate context -> Clarify what you do -> Clarify why relevant -> CTA
special_rules: One sentence restating the original context/reason for reaching out
One sentence clarifying specifically what Mintago does, in plain language, no jargon
One sentence on why this is relevant to this persona/seniority specifically
End with a call-to-conversation CTA, not a meeting ask

steps.label: referral_exit
steps.framework: Name-check possible better contact -> Explain why -> Restate original reason -> Close loop
special_rules: Ask if someone else at the company would be better placed to discuss this — only if plausible from the available data; otherwise use a soft 'wrong timing' exit instead
Briefly restate why you reached out originally
P.S. line nodding back to the original ask
No pressure, no urgency, no hard-breakup tone — a polite, low-pressure close

cross_sequence_rules: Only steps 1 and 3 may contain anything resembling a pitch
Never restate the same observation verbatim across emails — vary phrasing
Never more than one open-ended question per email
